Checking the answer before trusting it
A tool-using agent has idx_9f719144 two kinds of output. First, it has the raw tool results. Second, it has the
final model response. The final model response should never be treated as more authoritative
than the tool results.
If the tool output says one neighbor is Idle, but the final answer says all BGP peers are
established, the final answer is wrong. The agent sounded confident, but the evidence
disagreed. That is exactly the kind of failure production systems must catch.

Expanding the missing route investigation
A missing route to host idx_4509c110 symptom idx_c2494b25 should not immediately be blamed on BGP. The agent should
treat it as a symptom and gather supporting evidence. The exact route may be missing because
of BGP, static routing, filtering, an access control rule, or a host problem.
In this mocked lab, we can still teach the right habit. The agent can run a reachability check
and compare that with BGP and interface evidence. If the target is unreachable, leaf2 has an
idle neighbor with zero prefixes, and Ethernet3 is down, the agent can say BGP and the server-
facing interface are likely areas to investigate next.
The reachability result for an unknown target looks like this:

"target": "10.99.99.99",
"packets_sent": 4,
"packets_received": 0,
"packet_loss": 100,
"status": "unreachable",
"error": "Destination host unreachable"

This is not the same as proving a specific route is missing from a routing table. It is a
reachability symptom. A careful final answer should say exactly that. It can connect the
symptom to the BGP evidence, but it should not claim proof that is not in the tool output.

expose tools to clients. The business logic can stay in Python, but the client no longer needs to
know exactly how those functions are implemented. It can discover tools, call them through a
protocol, and receive structured results.

Managing Terraform state in a collaborative
environment
Our current workflow idx_8a095910 has a major flaw. When idx_9d19de6a GitHub Actions runs terraform apply, it
creates a terraform.tfstate file on the temporary runner. When the job finishes, the runner is
destroyed, and the state file is lost forever. The next time the pipeline runs, Terraform will have
no memory of the S3 bucket it created and will try to create it again, leading to an error. This is
the problem with local state.
To work in a team and in an automated pipeline, you must use idx_3e0de6e2 a remote backend. A remote
backend tells Terraform to store its state file in a shared, persistent location, such as an AWS S3
bucket. This provides a central source of truth for your infrastructure's state and enables
locking to prevent concurrent runs from corrupting the state. For stronger concurrent
protection, you can pair the S3 backend with an AWS DynamoDB table for state locking. When
configured, Terraform acquires a lock entry in DynamoDB before any operation and releases it
when done, ensuring two pipeline runs can never write to the state file simultaneously and
preventing state corruption in busy teams. Let's learn how to configure a remote backend.

The lifecycle as an iterative operating model
Development, training, deployment, and monitoring are often drawn in a straight line because
the order is easy to remember. In idx_ab4ed643 practice, the lifecycle behaves as a loop. A monitoring alert
may reveal that input data has changed. A deployment test may show that a model is accurate
but too slow. A training run may expose a data-quality problem that requires another
development pass. Each result can redirect the project to an earlier stage.
This iterative behavior changes the infrastructure requirement. Teams need environments that
can reproduce an earlier experiment, preserve model and data versions, and promote a known
artifact into production. They also need a traceable relationship among code, configuration,
training data, metrics, and deployed versions. Without that relationship, a team may know
that a model is failing but not be able to recreate the conditions that produced it.
The lifecycle is therefore both technical and collaborative. Data scientists need fast
experimentation, platform teams need controlled environments, and operations teams need
stable services. MLOps connects those interests by idx_20c6583d turning handoffs into managed workflows.

Training: Scaling compute and preserving evidence
Training takes the prototype and applies it to larger, production-scale datasets. The increase in

from interruption and must capture logs and metrics so that different runs can be compared
rather than judged from memory.
Experiment-tracking tools such as MLflow, Weights and Biases, or TensorBoard record
parameters, metrics, and artifacts. This evidence matters for both model quality and
infrastructure cost. A model that gains a small accuracy improvement while consuming
substantially more GPU time may not be the best production choice. Training operations
therefore balance model performance with duration, capacity, and cost.
At the end of training, the team should have more than a model file. It should have a versioned
artifact accompanied by checkpoints, metrics, logs, and enough configuration information to
explain how the artifact was produced. That package becomes the input to deployment.

artifact must be packaged and idx_a7ae0d53 exposed so that another application can request predictions.
The service may respond to real-time requests, as in a chatbot or recommendation system, or
process batches in an offline pipeline. The infrastructure must match the response pattern.
Real-time inference emphasizes low latency, consistent response time, and high availability.
Batch inference emphasizes throughput and efficient use of resources over a larger collection of
records. In either case, the model may be converted to an efficient format and placed behind an

MLOps as an operational discipline
MLOps extends DevOps ideas into a domain where data and models change independently of
application code. A conventional idx_d40d1400 deployment can often be reproduced from a source repository
and build definition. An AI deployment may also depend on a particular dataset version,
feature transformation, model configuration, checkpoint, framework version, and hardware
environment.
147 Operating the AI Lifecycle with MLOps and Inference
The discipline therefore emphasizes version control, reproducibility, audit trails, and
consistent promotion across environments. A team should be able to answer which code and
data produced a model, which metrics justified its promotion, which version is serving
production traffic, and how to roll back if the deployment fails. These questions require records
that span development and operations.
Automation reduces the chance that an undocumented manual step will break that chain. A
pipeline can ingest data, validate it, train a model, record metrics, run tests, register an artifact,
and deploy it only after approval. Monitoring can later start the same pipeline with new data.
The tools in the remainder of this section implement different parts of that operating model.
Apache Airflow for task orchestration
Apache Airflow orchestrates workflows that contain ordered and dependent tasks. A workflow
is represented as a directed idx_52c63d4e acyclic graph, or DAG. Each node represents work such as data
ingestion, cleaning, model training, evaluation, batch inference, or report generation. The
directed edges define which tasks must finish before another task can begin.
The acyclic property prevents a workflow from creating an endless dependency loop.
Repetition is handled through scheduling rather than by connecting a task back to itself.
Airflow can run a DAG on a timetable, monitor task status, retry failures, and expose the
execution history so that operators can see where a pipeline stopped.

None of these issues is visible through manual testing alone. They require structured

To make this concrete, consider idx_22f999e0 a well-documented case that became a reference point in AI

queries, including questions about bereavement travel policies. A passenger asked the chatbot
whether a discounted bereavement fare could be claimed after the trip. The chatbot said yes —
and even provided instructions for submitting the request within 90 days. The passenger
booked a full-price ticket based on that guidance and submitted the reimbursement request
afterward. The airline denied it. The actual policy did not allow retroactive claims.
The company argued it could not be held responsible for the chatbot's misleading information,
going as far as claiming the chatbot should be considered a separate entity — and therefore
absolved of any liability for its inaccuracies. The tribunal rejected that argument entirely,
finding that the airline owed the passenger a duty of care and had failed to exercise reasonable
care to ensure the chatbot's information was accurate and not misleading.
The technical failure was not dramatic. The model did not produce offensive content or go
wildly off-script. It generated a nonexistent policy — confidently, coherently, and in a context
where the user had every reason to trust it. That is precisely the kind of failure that manual
testing misses: it behaves correctly in most cases, sounds authoritative, and only breaks under
specific conditions unlikely to appear in a curated test dataset. Springer

Dynamic batching, concurrency, and model ensembles
Dynamic batching idx_4c5af346 allows Triton to combine compatible requests into a larger batch before
idx_f059d39c execution. A idx_30907051 GPU can often process a batch more efficiently than a sequence of small
independent requests because fixed launch and scheduling overhead is spread across more
work. The objective is to improve throughput while remaining inside the service latency target.
Concurrent model execution allows multiple models or model versions to run on the same
server. This is useful when a shared platform serves several teams or when a deployment must
compare a new version with the current one. Resource planning remains important because
concurrency can improve utilization but can also create contention if memory or compute
capacity is overcommitted.
Model ensembles connect several models or processing steps into one inference pipeline. A
request might be preprocessed, classified, and postprocessed without requiring the client to
coordinate each stage separately. The ensemble presents one service boundary while Triton
manages the internal sequence.
These capabilities idx_d2cadafe answer different performance problems. Dynamic batching improves the
idx_b2a5c224 execution of incoming requests, concurrency allows multiple model workloads idx_806b73a1 to coexist, and
ensembles compose a multi-step inference path. Triton also needs a controlled way to discover
and version the artifacts it serves.

TensorRT for GPU-optimized inference
TensorRT is NVIDIA's inference optimizer and runtime. It converts a supported trained model,
often through ONNX, into an engine tuned for NVIDIA GPUs. The optimization process can
reduce latency, increase throughput, and lower memory usage, making it possible to serve
more requests or models on the available hardware.
Precision idx_943b08ce calibration, graph optimization, kernel autotuning, and layer fusion are important
mechanisms. FP16 and INT8 reduce the amount of data used for suitable operations, while
graph and kernel optimization select more efficient execution paths. Layer fusion combines
operations where possible so that intermediate movement and launch overhead are reduced.
Precision is a performance and accuracy trade-off. A lower-precision engine may deliver
greater throughput and a smaller memory footprint, but the result must still meet the model's
quality requirement. Calibration and benchmarking are therefore part of the optimization
process rather than an afterthought.
TensorRT engines integrate with Triton, DeepStream, and NVIDIA edge platforms. The
operational pattern is to optimize once for the target environment and then serve the resulting
engine through a managed runtime.
The complete path from training to production inference
The end-to-end path brings the chapter together. A model is developed and trained in a chosen
framework. Its runs, parameters, metrics, and artifacts are tracked. The selected model is
registered and exported to ONNX when portability idx_d1ab951d is required. TensorRT then produces a GPU-
optimized engine, and Triton exposes that engine as a versioned service.
The deployment can run in a container and later be scaled with Kubernetes and Helm.
Monitoring captures request behavior and GPU telemetry. If latency rises, quality falls, or input
data changes, the evidence feeds the MLOps workflow and starts another development or
training iteration.

Architecture of a log dialogue pipeline
Before idx_4239ffd5idx_13bf9d19 writing code, it is worth mapping the components. A minimal log dialog pipeline for
Linux has four stages:
Collection: ship logs from /var/log/syslog, journalctl, audit.log, and dmesg into a
local buffer.
Chunking: split logs into time-windowed segments (e.g. five-minute buckets) so
prompts stay within model context limits.
Prompting: inject host, service, and time-window metadata into a structured prompt
template before sending to the model.
Response handling: parse the model reply to extract hypotheses, supporting evidence,
and suggested commands, then surface them to the engineer.

Setting thresholds that mean something
Evaluation scores in Foundry idx_58cc0d7c are typically expressed as values between 0 and 1 (or 1 to 5,
depending on the evaluator). The platform lets you define pass/fail thresholds per metric, but
the defaults are just starting points—you need to calibrate them against your use case.
A practical starting framework:
Metric Conservative threshold When to tighten it
Relevance ≥ 0.75 High-stakes or regulated domains
Groundedness ≥ 0.80 RAG apps, policy-driven assistants
Coherence ≥ 0.70 Customer-facing interfaces
Intent Resolution ≥ 0.75 Ambiguous or multi-intent inputs
Safety metrics ≥ 0.95 Always—no exceptions
Table 7.1: Suggested evaluation thresholds for deciding whether an AI deployment is ready for use
The key principle here is that safety thresholds should always be stricter than quality
thresholds. A Groundedness score of 0.72 in a low-risk internal tool is acceptable. The same
score in a healthcare or financial assistant is not.
When comparing two idx_fc5fe92f deployments, don't just look at which one scores higher overall. Look at
where each one fails. A model that scores 0.85 on average but drops to 0.40 on escalation
scenarios is a worse production candidate than one scoring 0.78 consistently across all
categories.
Balancing evaluation quality against cost
Every evaluation run idx_f32119f7 consumes tokens — both for generating responses from your target
model and for running the judge model that scores them. This adds up fast if you're not
intentional about it.
A few rules of thumb:
Dataset size matters more than you think. A 30-sample dataset is fine for a quick
smoke test after a prompt change. For a release decision or a model swap, aim for 100–
300 samples that cover your real traffic distribution — edge cases included.

Not all metrics cost the same. Safety evaluators tend to be lighter. Quality evaluators
like Coherence and Groundedness involve more judge model computation. Run safety
checks more frequently and reserve full-quality evaluations for significant changes.
Judge model selection has cost implications. Using a large model as your judge gives
you more reliable scores, but it costs more per evaluation run. For routine checks, a
smaller capable model is often sufficient. Reserve your best judge model for release-
gate evaluations.

things. The honest answer is, it depends on how often your system changes and how much risk

Figure 7.4: Binary bit place values in decimal
Since there are only 8 bits in binary per octet, the maximum place value for the far left bit you
can define is 2 to the power of 7 (2^7). This is because you start at 2 to the power of 0 (2^0) in
the far right.
Starting from the right and idx_1537af43 moving to the left, the value of each bit can be either a '0' or the
resulting power of 2 in decimal, based on the bit position. So, for example:
The first value of the first bit is either equal to '0' or '1'. If X is 1, it is 2 to the power of 0
(2^0), which is 1.
The second bit is double the first bit and is either equal to '0' or '2'. If X is 1, it is 2 to the
power of 1 (2 ^ 1), which is 2.
The third bit is double the second bit and is either equal to '0' or '4'. If X is 1, then it is 2
to the power 2 (2 ^ 2), which is 4.
The fourth bit is double the third bit and is either equal to '0' or '8'. If X is 1, then it is 2
to the power of 3 (2^3), which is 8, and so on.
To calculate the decimal values of the binary representation, you must first identify which of
the Xs should be converted to a '1' and which to '0' in binary. The decimal value is then derived
by adding up all the place values of each bit as follows:
Decimal = (X*128) + (X*64) + (X*32) + (X*16) + (X*8) + (X*4) + (X*2) + (X*1)
So, to calculate the binary representation of '7' from the IP address 192.168.1.7, you must
identify which of the 'Xs' should be converted to zeros and which ones to ones. You can only
convert those bits to ones whose value will be equal to or less than your decimal number.

Failure modes and fallback strategies
Production dialog pipelines encounter three primary failure modes that require explicit
handling rather than silent propagation. Understanding each failure type and its recovery path
is a prerequisite to responsible deployment idx_5a7e9760idx_c6a0f57b of any AI-assisted observability workflow.
Bad suggestions occur when the model returns a hypothesis that is syntactically valid but
operationally incorrect — plausible-sounding but not supported by the evidence. Mitigation:
require the model to cite specific log lines or metric values for every hypothesis, and reject any
hypothesis whose cited evidence cannot be located in the provided context. Set a minimum
confidence threshold (typically 0.60) below which the pipeline surfaces all hypotheses as "low
confidence — human review required" rather than presenting a single recommendation.
Partial actions occur when a multi-step remediation plan succeeds through step N but fails at
step N+1, leaving the system in an indeterminate state. Mitigation: treat each approved
remediation plan as an atomic transaction. Before each step, re-validate that the preconditions
established by prior steps still hold. If any validation fails mid-plan, halt immediately, record
the partial execution state to the audit log with a REQUIRES_HUMAN_REVIEW flag, and page
the on-call engineer with the complete step-by-step audit trail.

The following standard classes have the following configurations:
Class A: The first octet (first 8 bits) of a class A address represents the network portion,
where the remaining three octets (24 bits) define the host portion. Furthermore, the
first bit of a Class A network is always set to '0' in binary since the IP range for a Class A
starts at '0'. The remaining 7 bits in the first octet define the number of networks idx_a548ff32 in this
class. Thus, taking 2 to the power of 7 (2^7) will give you 128, the total number of
possible networks you can have in a Class A. It is important to remember that two
networks within this range cannot be used to host devices. The first network is
0.0.0.0, and the second is 127.0.0.0 (up to 127.255.255.255). This is because:
0.0.0.0 represents a reference point rather than a network. It means a default
route and is used to signify any network, like a wildcard for routing purposes.
127.0.0.0 is known as the loopback address and is used for local communication
within a device. Any data packet sent to 127.x.x.x never leaves the device – it is
often used for troubleshooting or testing applications locally.
The total number of possible host machines in a Class A network is calculated as
follows: (2^24) - 2 = 16,777,214. You must subtract 2 IP addresses because the first IP
address represents the network ID, and the last IP address represents the broadcast IP.
Class B: The first two octets (first 16 bits) of a class B address define the network
portion, and the remaining 16 bits can be used for the host portion. The first two bits
are also set to 10 in a class B network, meaning that this class's starting IP address is
128. This means the remaining 14 bits (16 minus the two bits set to '10') define the
number of networks in a Class B range. Therefore, the total possible networks you can
have in a Class B is 16,384 (2^14).
The remaining 16 bits are used for possible host IP addresses and are calculated as
follows: (2^16) - 2 = 65,534. You must subtract 2 IP addresses because the first IP
address represents the network ID, and the last IP address represents the broadcast IP
address per network in this class.
Class C: The first three idx_61bf82d4 octets (first 24 bits) of a Class C address define the network
portion, and the remaining 8 bits represent the host portion. In a Class C network, the
first three far-left bits are set to 110, meaning that this class's starting range of IP
addresses is 192. Furthermore, the remaining 21 bits define the number of networks in a
Class C. This gives you 2,097,152 (2 ^ 21) possible networks.
The remaining 8 bits are used for possible host IP addresses and are calculated as
follows: (2^8) - 2 = 254. Again, remember that the first IP address in the network is the
network ID, and the last IP address is used for broadcast traffic.

What is subnetting?
Previously, you used fixed-length subnet idx_0453ceb4 masks to mask off portions of your IP address to
define network and host portions. You would mask off the first octet of the IP address for a
Class A network, the first two octets for a Class B network, and the first three octets for a Class
C network. So, for a class A network, you could use the subnet mask 255.0.0.0 to mask off the
first octet of your IP address for the network portion. Any changes in the first octet of an IP
address would yield a different network. For example, when using a subnet mask of 255.0.0.0,
the IP address 10.0.0.0 is on a different network than 31.0.0.0.
Subnetting is a process by which you can use a subnet mask to divide a more extensive network
into smaller subnetworks (subnets). This is particularly useful when you have different workload
types that need to be isolated from each other, or you want to reduce broadcast traffic,
allowing only permitted network connections between these workloads. For example, you
have a more extensive corporate network and want subnetworks for your backend databases,
frontend web servers, and a network for your employee workforce.
Subnetting involves borrowing bits from the host portion of an IP address range to create these
smaller subnetworks. These borrowed bits effectively enable you to create subsets of your
larger primary network. The subnetworks are therefore part of the larger primary network, but
traffic between the subnetworks can be restricted to ensure isolation of workloads, enhance
security, and ensure operational efficiency.
Take the example of a business that needs eight subnetworks, each capable of hosting 30 IP
addresses for a maximum of 30 devices idx_109f3352 per network. The company could use a standard Class
C IP address range of 192.168.0.0, with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0. The resulting eight
networks could be:

Patterns for AI-Assisted Troubleshooting
Ad-hoc prompts written under pressure at 3 a.m. produce inconsistent, unreliable answers.
The solution is to encode your idx_0cf8c542idx_36e71a85 team's diagnostic expertise into reproducible prompt patterns
— structured templates that combine the right context, the right questions, and the right
output format for each category of incident. This section defines five production-grade
troubleshooting patterns that every SRE team should have in their toolkit: OOM and memory
pressure, CPU saturation, disk and I/O pressure, network degradation, and application crash
and stack-trace analysis.
Each pattern follows the same engineering structure: a typed Python dataclass that captures
the diagnostic context, a prompt template that encodes SRE expertise, integration with the
Operations RAG pipeline built in Section 7.2, and measurable MTTR impact. Together they
form a Diagnostic Pattern Library — a shared asset that compounds in value as the team adds
incidents and runbooks to the knowledge base.

information must be idx_141a9bb6idx_72fed608 collected before the model is invoked), a prompt template (how that
information is presented to the model), an output contract (what structure the model must
return), and a metric hook (how the result updates MTTR tracking).
The difference between an ad-hoc prompt and a reproducible pattern is the same as the
difference between a bash one-liner and an Ansible playbook: one solves a problem once, the
other solves it reliably at scale, by any team member, with auditable results.

At the beginning of this chapter, you discovered how corporate networks are divided into
smaller subnetworks. In AWS, when idx_052e6e93 you build VPCs, you deploy certain specific resources in

security. By deploying resources in a private subnet, you ensure they are not idx_6956ddac directly accessible

should only be accessible through frontend web servers or load balancers. This setup ensures
that any traffic to backend services is proxied through frontend web servers, preventing direct
exposure to the Internet.
However, some application servers in private subnets still require Internet access, for example,
to download software updates, security patches, or product updates. Since these servers do not
have public IP addresses, you need a mechanism idx_55b7f713 to allow outbound Internet access. This is
where Network Address Translation (NAT) comes in.

routes the traffic to the idx_69b99e94 Internet.

access to the internet on ports 80 and 443, the responses to those requests will automatically
be allowed inbound. Conversely, suppose you define an inbound rule to allow users from the

corresponding outbound responses are automatically permitted.

rules before any traffic can reach the resources attached to the Security Group. Additionally,
explicit deny rules cannot be configured.

A VPC peering connection is a private network link between two VPCs, allowing resources in

When multi-agent orchestration is worth it
Multi-agent orchestration is idx_ab3e52d4 worth using when an incident requires different expertise
domains, for example, triage combined with runbook lookup, fix planning, and risk review,
each of which benefits from a specialist. It is also worth using when parallelism and
independent checks matter: agents don't need to run sequentially; they can fan out and run in
parallel on their individual tasks before converging on a final solution.
The outcome should be a structured consensus, a package combining the results from each
agent, not a single opinion.
Orchestration patterns
There are different ways to orchestrate multiple agents:
Sequential orchestration: A idx_78205bd7 controlled handoff, where agent A runs and hands off to
agent B, agent C, and idx_5fafb977 so on.
Concurrent orchestration: Allows idx_5a92350c for parallel idx_d7cd73bc evidence gathering.
Hybrid fan-out/fan-in orchestration: Independent idx_14300510 specialists run concurrently, after
which their outputs are idx_b6ee80fc aggregated and passed to a coordinating agent or deterministic
function for controlled synthesis.
Free-form group chat should be avoided for urgent operational paths. Use explicit contracts,
structured outputs, and a human approval gate before any production-changing or otherwise
high-impact action is taken.
Multi-agent systems typically start with an event trigger, an alert, or a failure. An event router
handles subscriptions and filters, deliveries and retries, and dead-lettering for failed deliveries,
ensuring that any information that fails to be delivered is properly handled.
Safety boundaries and guardrails
Multi-agent systems should follow the same safety principles idx_9408aec5 established for single agents
throughout this book:
Agents are read-only by default, without idx_3f32104f autonomy to make production changes.
A human approves production-changing or otherwise high-impact actions; read-only
evidence gathering can remain automated within defined boundaries.
Tool access and credentials are limited by role.

Lessons Learned
Measure before you build, not after: The teams that get the most value from AI-assisted
observability are the ones that establish baseline DORA metrics, MTTR measurements,
and alert precision/recall scores before they deploy the first model. Without a baseline,
you cannot prove improvement — and without proof, the system will not survive the
next budget cycle.
Context quality determines answer quality, not model size: A well-structured prompt
with host name, service name, time window, and relevant log lines from a 7B
parameter local model will outperform a poorly structured prompt sent to a 70B
model. The architectural work of this chapter — context dataclasses, time-window
chunkers, typed pattern schemas — is more important than model selection.
Fewer, better alerts outperform more, louder ones: Every non-actionable alert that fires
erodes engineer trust in the alerting system. Once engineers stop trusting alerts, they
take longer to respond to real ones. The AI layer's primary job is not to generate more
signals — it is to compress many signals into one actionable diagnosis. Guard this
ruthlessly.
RAG is only as good as your documentation discipline: A vector store full of stale
runbooks, undated incident reports, and TODO comments will make the model
confidently wrong. Treat your operations knowledge base with the same discipline you
apply to production code: review it, version it, test it, and retire outdated entries. The
indexing pipeline is the enforcer — automate the quality gate.
The human approval gate is not optional: Every remediation command that the AI
suggests must pass through a human decision point before execution. This is not a
limitation of current models — it is the correct architecture for any system that acts on
production infrastructure. The AI earns the right to suggest; the engineer retains the
right to decide.
Evaluate your anomaly detectors monthly, not annually: Workloads change. A detector
calibrated in January will drift by March. The AnomalyEvaluator from Section 7.4.3
costs five minutes to run monthly; a false-negative that misses a production outage
costs hours. Schedule the evaluation as a monthly cron job and alert on detector quality
degradation the same way you alert on service degradation.
Structured outputs are not optional ,they are infrastructure: The difference between an
AI system that integrates into your operations workflow and one that requires an
engineer to read prose responses is a JSON schema. Every idx_2d50c3abidx_ff8e6a46 pattern in this chapter

enough to be useful.
This is exactly where Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) becomes valuable, enabling
faster incident triage, producing grounded answers based on real system data, and providing
auditable evidence by linking responses back to logs, configuration files, and documentation.
In Chapter 2, you explored the distinction between traditional ML methods and LLMs. We left
an open question: what happens when the amount of data you need to reason over is massive?
A classic ML model can process large datasets, but it often requires heavy preprocessing,
retraining, and careful feature engineering. As data grows, it can become slow, brittle, or even
overfit to patterns that don't generalize. On the other hand, LLMs are great at capturing long-
range dependencies and reasoning across text, but they have a hard limit: the context window.
Even though context sizes are getting bigger, you still can't just dump terabytes of logs or
documentation into a prompt and expect a useful answer. In practice, this limitation is
addressed through techniques such as chunking data into smaller pieces, retrieving only the
most relevant context, and summarizing information before passing it to the model.

The following section provides a summary of this chapter.
Summary
AWS Virtual Private Cloud is a service that enables you to build secure, isolated networks in
your AWS account to host your application workloads. This allows you to separate workloads
for various reasons, including compliance and security. A VPC spans an entire AWS region,
enabling access to all Availability Zones (AZs) within that region to host your applications.
You create subnets within specific AZs, allowing you to define subnetworks in the VPC when
deploying your applications. This setup lets you host replica workloads across multiple
subnets and AZs, enhancing high availability in case of an AZ outage.
Multiple VPCs within a region or across different regions can be connected using VPC Peering,
which enables routing traffic between VPCs over AWS's private network. This reduces costs
associated with internet traffic and enhances security. You can also host different components
of your applications across multiple VPCs—for example, compute services in one VPC with a
peering connection to another VPC hosting backend databases. This approach adds security
layers by restricting access to specific VPCs based on administrative and engineering needs. For
example, you might ensure that database administrators only have access to VPCs hosting
databases while restricting access to web servers.
For more complex network connectivity, AWS offers the VPC Transit Gateway, which
provides a hub-and-spoke model to connect multiple VPCs. This eliminates the need for
individual peering connections, reducing operational complexity.
You can also connect your VPCs to on-premises locations using VPNs or AWS Direct Connect.
The latter provides higher bandwidth and routes traffic over private networks, bypassing the
public internet entirely.
Ultimately, VPCs are designed to help you build secure, private networks in the cloud, isolating
workloads and ensuring that only authorized inbound and outbound traffic reaches your
applications.

AWS Compute Services – EC2,

At the core of every application lies a compute resource — the technology that powers
computational processing and data operations. Computing capacity has evolved significantly
over time. In the early days, this was provided by physical servers. A server is a computer or
software system that delivers resources, services, or data to other computers, known as clients,
over a network. However, physical servers had limited processing power, memory, and storage
capacity. Due to these constraints—and challenges related to application compatibility, such
as shared libraries and runtime environments—businesses typically dedicate a single physical
server to each application. As a result, organizations maintained large banks of servers to
support their various business applications, often requiring significant real estate, either on-
premises or in co-located data centers, to accommodate their extensive infrastructure.
With the advent of virtualization and an increase in compute resources such as CPU (Central
Processing Unit) capacity, memory, and storage, it was now possible to host multiple virtual
machines (virtual servers) on a single physical host machine. This means that you can now run
multiple applications on a single physical server, all isolated from each other within their own
virtual machines. This avoided compatibility issues while reducing the overall footprint of
physical hardware.
In this chapter, you will explore Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2). This service enables
you to deploy virtual machines, providing the compute capacity needed to run applications
ranging from simple websites to advanced artificial intelligence and data analytics workloads.
Additionally, you will learn about other AWS compute services, including containerization,
which offers a more efficient alternative to traditional virtual machines, and serverless
architectures powered by event-driven compute services, which significantly reduce
administrative overhead and provide a highly cost-effective solution.

Building a Network Co-Pilot
When I started in the field as a junior network engineer, I had lots of questions, and I mean lots
of questions! Many of the answers could be found in books and online resources, but it took so
long to search through different sources and piece together the answer. Other times, the answer
took the form of tribal knowledge, meaning I had to spend hours looking through the current
configuration and ask more senior engineers, and then – maybe – get a decent answer. In short,
I wish I’d had a network co-pilot who could help me filter out answers, understand the network,
answer my questions at all hours, and just be my network best friend.
Well, this chapter focuses on building such a pal. Think of a network co-pilot as your AI assistant
that understands networking with the network data you are willing to supply. Instead of reading
through countless documentation and CLI commands, you can have a conversation with your
co-pilot: “Help me configure OSPF on this Cisco router,” or “Why does the interface error counter
keep on incrementing at midnight, every other Wednesday?”
A good network co-pilot does not replace a network engineer’s expertise; it amplifies it. It helps
us work faster, catches mistakes, and makes suggestions to help us get more done.
In this chapter, we will build the core components that make a network co-pilot work. We are
not building a full production app (because that would take another book to do so!), but we will
create the essential pieces that show you how it all fits together.

while the permissions of a Role are grouped together for a specific function, that function is defined
at a lower, technical level than “enterprise” roles.
Now that we’ve differentiated between what the “enterprise” definition of a role is from how Kuber-
netes defines a Role, let’s dive into how you build a Role.
Each resource that a role will be built from is identified by the following:
• apiGroups: A list of groups the resources are a member of
• resources: The name of the object type for the resource (and potentially sub-resources)
• resourceNames: An optional list of specific objects to apply this rule to
Each rule must have a list of apiGroups and resources. resourceNames is optional.
Once the resource is identified in a rule, verbs can be specified. A verb is an action that can be taken
on the resource, providing access to the object in Kubernetes.
If the desired access to an object should be all, you do not need to add each verb; instead, the wildcard
character may be used to identify all the verbs, resources, or apiGroups.
Identifying a Role
The Kubernetes authorization page (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/
rbac/) uses the following Role as an example to allow someone to get the details of a pod and its logs:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
namespace: default
name: pod-and-pod-logs-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
verbs: ["get", "list"]
Before defining what a Role manages, it’s important to note that Role objects are namespaced, so
the namespace the Role is created in means that the permissions it defines apply only within its own
namespace. In this example, the Role only applies to the default namespace.
Working backward to determine how this Role was defined, we will start with resources, since it is the
easiest aspect to find. All objects in Kubernetes are represented by URLs. If you wanted to pull all the in-
formation about the pods in the default namespace, you would call the /api/v1/namespaces/default/
pods URL, and if you wanted the logs for a specific pod, you would call the /api/v1/namespaces/
default/pods/mypod/log URL.
RBAC Policies and Auditing 222
The URL pattern will be true of all namespace-scoped objects. pods lines up to resources, as does
pods/log. When trying to identify which resources you want to authorize, use the api-reference
document from the Kubernetes API documentation at https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/#api-

Negative Roles
One of the most common requests for authorization is “ Can I write a Role that lets me do everything EX-
CEPT xyz?”. In RBAC, the answer is NO. RBAC requires either every resource to be allowed or specific
resources and verbs to be enumerated. There are two reasons for this in RBAC:
• Better security through simplicity: Being able to enforce a rule that says every Secret except this
one requires a much more complex evaluation engine than RBAC provides. The more complex
an engine, the harder it is to test and validate, and the easier it is to break. A simpler engine
is just simpler to code and keep secure.
• Unintended consequences: Allowing someone to do everything except xyz leaves the door open
for issues in unintended ways as the cluster grows and new capabilities are added.
On the first point, an engine with this capability is difficult to build and maintain. It also makes the
rules much harder to keep track of. To express this type of rule, you need to not only have authori-
zation rules but also an order to those rules. For instance, to say I want to allow everything except this
Secret, you would first need a rule that says allow everything and then a rule that says deny this secret.
If you switch the rules to say deny this secret then allow everything, the first rule would be overridden.
You could assign priorities to different rules, but that now makes it even more complex.
There are ways to implement this pattern, either by using a custom authorization webhook or by using
a controller to dynamically generate RBAC Role objects. These should both be considered security
anti-patterns and so won’t be covered in this chapter.

OpenSSH client
The client part of OpenSSH has its system-wide defaults in the /usr/etc/ssh/ssh_config file.
You can add system-wide customizations to it in the files in the /etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/ folder.
Users can also have personal configuration in the ~/.ssh/config file.
Usually, the system-wide file just contains some comments, not actual settings, so we will be
focusing on the per-user configuration file and command-line parameters.
One example entry in our ~/.ssh/config file could be as follows:
Host jump
Hostname jump.example.com
User root
Compression yes
StrictHostKeyChecking no
ProxyCommand connect-proxy -H squid.example.com:3128 %h %p
ControlPath ~/.ssh/master-%r@%h:%p
ControlMaster auto
In the previous example, we defined an entry named jump (which we can use with ssh jump) that
will connect the root username to the jump.example.com host.
This is a basic setting, but we’re also defining that we’ll be using a helper program in ProxyCommand
that will make use of a proxy server on squid.example.com on port 3128 to connect to the %h
host and the %p port to reach our target system. Additionally, we’re making use of Compression to
compress and decompress the data sent and received, and using ControlMaster to share multiple
sessions with one single connection.
One feature that has security implications is StrictHostKeyChecking. When we connect to a host
for the first time, keys are exchanged between the client and the host, and the server identifies
itself with the keys that are used. If they’re accepted, they will be stored in the .ssh/known_hosts
file at the user’s home directory.
The ~ directory is an alias for the user’s home directory. You can identify which one
it is by running echo $HOME. For regular users, it is often a folder with the name of
the user under /home.
Administering Systems Remotely 226
If the remote host key is changed, a warning will be printed on the SSH client’s terminal, and
the connection will be refused. However, if we set StrictHostKeyChecking to no, we will accept
any key that’s sent by the server, which might be useful if we’re using a test system that gets
redeployed frequently (and thus, generates a new host key). It is not recommended to be used in
general, since it protects us from a server being replaced and also from someone impersonating
the server we want to connect to with a server that, for example, logs usernames and passwords
to access our system later.
In the next section, we will learn about accessing remote systems with SSH.

systems. In general, the syntax, in its most basic form, is just executing the ssh command in your
terminal, adding a hostname or IP address after it, to indicate to which system we should connect.

RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings
Once a permission is defined, it needs to be assigned to something to enable it. “Something” can be
a user, a group, or a service account. These options are referred to as subjects. Just as with Roles
and ClusterRoles, a RoleBinding binds a Role or ClusterRole to a specific namespace, and a
ClusterRoleBinding will apply a ClusterRole across the cluster. A binding can have many subjects
but may only reference a single Role or ClusterRole. To assign the pod-and-pod-logs-reader Role
created earlier in this chapter to a service account called mysa in the default namespace, a user named
podreader, or anyone with the podreaders group, create a RoleBinding:

kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
name: pod-and-pod-logs-reader
namespace: default
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
name: mysa
namespace: default
apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: User

name: podreader
- kind: Group
name: podreaders

kind: Role

• ServiceAccount: Any service account in the cluster can be authorized to a RoleBinding. The

• Group: Just as with users, groups are asserted as part of the authentication process and have

measures depending on the nature of the issue, which may include restarting services,
adjusting configurations, updating software or hardware, or optimizing resource allocation,
etc.

into log management and operations processes, serving as the basis for adjusting and
optimizing alert settings, analysis procedures, and response strategies

tools and processes to ensure an immediate response when issues are detected. Automation

Till now, the focus has been on combining a Role with a RoleBinding and a ClusterRole with a
ClusterRoleBinding. If you want to define the same permissions that are scoped to multiple name-
spaces, you’ll want a way to do that without reproducing the same Role every time. Next, we’ll cover
how to simplify Role management by combining ClusterRoles and RoleBindings.
Combining ClusterRoles and RoleBindings
We have a use case where a log aggregator wants to pull logs from pod in multiple namespaces, but
not all namespaces. A ClusterRoleBinding is too broad. While the Role could be recreated in each
namespace, this is inefficient and a maintenance headache. Instead, define a ClusterRole but reference
it from a RoleBinding in the applicable namespaces. This allows the reuse of permission definitions
while still applying those permissions to specific namespaces. In general, note the following:
• ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding = cluster-wide permission
• ClusterRole + RoleBinding = namespace-specific permission
To apply our ClusterRoleBinding in a specific namespace, create a Role, referencing the ClusterRole
instead of a namespaced Role object:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
name: pod-and-pod-logs-reader
namespace: default
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
name: mysa
namespace: default
apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: User
name: podreader
- kind: Group
name: podreaders
roleRef:
kind: ClusterRole
name: cluster-pod-and-pod-logs-reader
apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
The preceding RoleBinding lets us reuse the existing ClusterRole. This cuts down on the number
of objects that need to be tracked in the cluster and makes it easier to update permissions across the
cluster if the ClusterRole permissions need to change.

prise identities into cluster policies.

(1) Data preprocessing
Before using machine learning algorithms, log data needs to be preprocessed. The steps include
data cleaning (removing irrelevant data, correcting erroneous data), normalization (unifying
log formats), feature extraction (extracting meaningful information from logs as input to the
model), etc. Effective data preprocessing can greatly improve the efficiency of model training
and prediction accuracy.
(2) Feature engineering
Feature engineering is a vital part of machine learning, involving the selection, modification, and
creation of new features to enhance model performance. In log analysis, common features include
the timestamp of log entries, source IP addresses, error codes, operation codes, etc. Advanced
features include keywords or phrases extracted from log text or statistical information based on
the event frequency within a time window.
(3) Selecting appropriate machine learning models
Selecting suitable machine learning models according to the characteristics of the log data and
business needs is essential. For anomaly detection, commonly used algorithms include clustering
algorithms, distance-based anomaly detection, and neural networks.
Typical clustering algorithms include K-means and DBSCAN. These unsupervised learning
algorithms can help identify natural groups in the data, with outliers usually not belonging to
any main group. In distance-based anomaly detection, typical examples are the Isolation Forest
algorithm and the LOF (Local Outlier Factor) algorithm, which identify anomalies by considering
the distance between data points and their neighbors. Among neural networks, autoencoders are
a typical example, mainly suitable for handling large-scale data sets and complex data structures.
They can learn the normal patterns of data and identify anomalous data that deviate from these
patterns.

Creating an audit policy
A policy file is used to control what events are recorded and where to store the logs, which can be a
standard log file or a webhook. We have included an example audit policy in the chapter7 directory
of the GitHub repository, and we will apply it to the KinD cluster that we have been using throughout
the book.
An audit policy is a collection of rules that tell the API server which API calls to log and how. When
Kubernetes parses the policy file, all rules are applied in order and only the initial matching policy event
will be applied. If you have more than one rule for a certain event, you may not receive the expected
data in your log files. For this reason, you need to be careful that your events are created correctly.
Policies use the audit.k8s.io API and the manifest kind of Policy. The following example shows
the beginning of a policy file:
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
- level: Request
userGroups: ["system:nodes"]
verbs: ["update","patch"]
resources:
- group: "" # core
resources: ["nodes/status", "pods/status"]
omitStages:
- "RequestReceived"
While a policy file may look like a standard Kubernetes manifest, you do not apply it using kubectl. A
policy file is used with the --audit-policy-file API flag on the API server(s). This will be explained
in the Enabling auditing on a cluster section.
To understand the rule and what it will log, we will go through each section in detail.
The first section of the rule is level, which determines the type of information that will be logged for
the event. There are four levels that can be assigned to events:
Table 7.1: Kubernetes auditing levels

The userGroups, verbs, and resources values tell the API server the object and action that will trigger
the auditing event. In this example, only requests from system:nodes that attempt an action of update
or patch on a node/status or pod/status on the core API will create an event.
omitStages tells the API server to skip any logging events during a stage, which helps you limit the
amount of data that is logged. There are four stages that an API request goes through:
Table 7.2: Auditing stages
In our example, we have set the event to ignore the RequestReceived event, which tells the API server
not to log any data for the incoming API request.

Understanding the LogFormer workflow
LogFormer addresses the above issues in two working phases: the Log Attention Encoding Phase
and the Cross-domain Adapter Fine-tuning Phase.
Preserving log semantics with Log Attention
The Log Attention Encoding Phase preserves semantic knowledge shared between different
domains. Specifically, to avoid information loss caused by log pattern parsing, the Log Attention
module models log sequences and makes additional use of parameter information that is neglected
in log pattern parsing, thereby achieving better performance. Compared to traditional structures,
the model additionally incorporates parameter information lost during log pattern parsing. The
LogFormer model structure is depicted in Figure 7.4, with the left part showing multi-head
encoding and the right part showing parameter encoding.

If we decide to create an SSH key with a password to protect it (good choice), we will need to input

convenient and reduces the chances of someone watching while you type in your key.

3. Then, we log out, and the connection is closed.
4. Next, we try to add the key, and we get an error because we have not set the environment
variables for the agent.
5. As instructed when we introduced the agent, we execute the command for loading the
environment variables for the agent in the current shell.
6. When we try to add the key with ssh-add withpass, the agent asks for our password.
7. When we finally ssh to the host, we can connect without a password as the key is in
memory for our key pair.
Here, we have achieved two things: we now have an automated/unattended method to connect
to systems and have ensured that only authorized users will know the password to unlock them.

Several services were replaced with SSH on many systems, and one of them was the insecure
protocol for file transfer known as File Transfer Protocol (FTP). It uses a communication that
transfers data in plain text, and it was a perfect target for intercepting credentials. FTP is hardly
ever used today, and where it is, it is mostly for serving publicly available files on servers that
only allow anonymous access.
SSH by default enables two interfaces for copying files: scp and sftp. The first one is used in a
similar way to the regular cp command, but here, we’re accepting remote hosts as our target or
source, while sftp uses a client approach similar to the traditional ftp command that interacts
with FTP servers. Just remember that in both cases, the connection is encrypted and happens
over port 22/tcp on the target host.

tween systems using the ssh layer for the whole process. This allows us to securely transfer a
file’s contents, plus all the automation capabilities that were introduced by key pair login, to

In addition to the main experimental results, Yunzhihui also conducted data ablation experiments.
To verify the effectiveness of pre-training, the performance of LogFormer-s and LogFormer-p

Experiments have proven that pre-training can accelerate convergence without sacrificing
performance, but fine-tuning is usually costly and important. Therefore, in the experiments,
Yunzhihui adopted adapter-based fine-tuning, which adds extra trainable parameters to obtain
a compact model for log anomaly detection. To verify the effectiveness of adapter-based fine-
tuning, LogFormer-p was compared with LogFormer on the HDFS and Thunderbird datasets.
As shown in Figure 7.9, the F1 value generated by LogFormer (with an average increase of 1%) is
slightly higher than direct fine-tuning of the pre-trained model on both datasets. In addition,
adapter-based fine-tuning used only 3.5% to 5.5% of trainable parameters, requiring very few
parameter adjustments.

Transferring files with rsync
Although we can use the -r option of scp to transfer files recursively, scp only handles the full
copy of the file, which is not ideal if we are just keeping some folders in sync across systems.
In 1996, rsync was launched, and many systems implemented it by using a dedicated server that
was listening to client connections. This was to allow full directory trees to be synchronized with
files. This was done by copying over the differences between the files. Here, we compared parts
of the source and destination to see whether there were differences that should be copied over.
With SSH, and with the rsync package installed on both the client and the server, we can take
advantage of the secure channel that’s created by SSH and the faster synchronization provided
by rsync.
The difference between using the rsync daemon and using SSH is the syntax for the source or
destination, which either uses the rsync:// protocol or :: after the hostname. In other cases, it
will use SSH or even the local filesystem.

Challenges and considerations when testing applications

Next to all the many advantages that testing applications running in containers brings to the table, we also need to
have a brief i d x _ b 7 a 5 0 4 0 b discussion of the challenges and considerations involved in this type of testing, such as dealing with
dependencies and managing test data:
Isolation: Testing applications in containers can provide a level of isolation between the test
environment and the host system, which can be useful for ensuring that the test results are consistent
and repeatable. However, this isolation can also make it more difficult to debug issues and identify the
root cause of problems, as you may not have access to the host system and its resources.
Environment consistency: Ensuring that the test environment is consistent across different
development environments can be a challenge when using containers. Differences in the host system,
container runtime, and network configuration can all impact the behavior of the application and the test
results.
Data management: Managing test data in a containerized environment can be challenging, as you may
need to ensure that the test data is consistent and available to all containers, or that it is properly isolated
and not shared between tests.
Resource constraints: Testing applications in containers can be resource-intensive, as you may need to
run multiple containers in parallel to test different scenarios. This can lead to resource contention and
may require careful resource management to ensure that your tests are reliable and consistent.
Integration testing: Testing the integration between multiple containers can be challenging, as you may
need to coordinate the startup and shutdown of multiple containers and ensure that they i d x _ 5 1 b 4 3 3 9 e can
communicate with each other.
Performance testing: Testing the performance of applications running in containers can be difficult, as
the performance may be impacted by the host system, the container runtime, and the network
configuration.
Overall, testing applications running in containers requires careful planning and consideration to ensure that the
test environment is consistent and reliable, and to ensure that the test results are meaningful and actionable.

tmux is a terminal multiplexer, which means that it allows us to open and access several terminals
within a single screen. A good similitude would be a window manager in a graphical desktop,
which allows us to open several windows so that we can switch context while using only one
monitor.
tmux also allows us to detach and reattach to the sessions, so it’s the perfect tool in case our
connection drops. Think, for example, about performing a software upgrade on a server. If, for
whatever reason, the connection drops, it will be equivalent to abruptly stopping the upgrade
process in whatever status it was at that moment, which can lead to bad consequences. However,
if the upgrade was launched inside tmux, the command will continue executing, and once the con-
nection is restored, the session can be reattached, and the output will be available to be examined.

of tmux is not to install it on our system (even if this is useful), but for it to be available on the
servers we connect to, to get that extra layer of protection in case a disconnection happens. So,
it’s a good habit to get used to installing it on all the servers we connect to.

Intelligent O&M tickets bring together several capabilities discussed earlier in the chapter:

understand how LLM agents can improve ticket handling, it is useful to first look at the role
tickets play in O&M workflows, then examine why general-purpose LLMs are not sufficient on

The role of intelligent O&M tickets
O&M ticket management is an important part of O&M services and a commonly used basic service
within O&M organizations. In the O&M service process, if users want to know the progress and
handling comments after submitting an incident ticket, they need to check the solution status and
handling comments of the nodes on the ticket details page. When O&M engineers are handling
tickets, they need to view the basic information of the incident ticket submitted by the user or
review the ticket information processed by previous nodes, which requires looking at the event’s
basic information fields, the solution status, and the handling comments of previous nodes.
O&M managers, when wanting to know the solution status and solutions of different nodes for
an incident ticket, need to check the form information of different nodes. For all users of the ticket
management process, if they need to understand the overview information of an incident ticket,
they all need to spend time viewing the relevant form fields. Existing O&M service management
tools lack a way for users to quickly grasp ticket information.
Tools by capability
LLM-assisted ticket handling is usually integrated with existing IT service manage -
ment, incident management, or on-call platforms. Common platforms include Jira
Service Management, ServiceNow, PagerDuty, and Opsgenie. In these environments,
LLM agents can help summarize ticket content, classify incidents, retrieve relevant
knowledge-base articles, suggest next steps, call internal APIs, and route tickets to
the right team or workflow.
The ticketing platform remains the system of record, while the LLM agent provides an
intelligence layer for understanding, summarizing, and acting on ticket information.

Challenges of current O&M LLM technology
In the design of intelligent O&M tickets, empowering O&M businesses with LLM-related
technologies requires solving two problems: first, how to teach LLMs to handle actual O&M
business, and second, how to balance stability and flexibility in the models. The main challenge
in choosing a technical path is that LLMs only possess general capabilities and are difficult to
use directly for specific business problems.
This challenge is easier to see in business-service scenarios where the model must not only
understand the user’s request, but also call internal systems and follow organization-specific
rules. Taking the operator’s O&M customer service scenario as an example, when a customer
inquires, such as “My phone number is 130XXXXXXXX, my name is John Doe, and the last six
digits of my ID are 000000. Please check my phone bill,” the typical reply from a general-purpose
GPT model is shown in Figure 7.19.
Figure 7.19: Example of a generic GPT reply
A general LLM can understand concepts such as phone numbers and names, and can recognize the
user’s need to query their phone bill, but does not yet possess the professional business capabilities
of an operator O&M customer service agent. Therefore, in applying LLMs to actual O&M business,
the core issue is how to cultivate their ability to solve real O&M business problems based on their
general knowledge. In intelligent O&M ticket scenarios, intelligent agent technology can endow
LLMs with the ability to execute business logic and call tools.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 254
In addition, the advantage of LLMs lies in their outstanding generalization ability, meaning they
can flexibly respond to different input information and process it accordingly. However, from a
technical standpoint, no LLM can guarantee solving all problems 100% of the time. Therefore,
in the intelligent O&M ticket scenario, rational system design is still required to ensure that the
LLM agent has both the stability and flexibility to handle problems.
An O&M LLM framework based on agent technology
Based on the intelligent O&M ticket scenario, YunZhiHui has designed an agent framework called
the multi-level API selector. The framework, as shown in Figure 7.20, mainly consists of four parts:
1. Pattern Recognition: Follows rule matching and executes the matched model according
to established logic
2. Semantic Retrieval: Establishes a preset ticket knowledge base, vectorizes the contents
of the ticket database and user requests via embedding, and retrieves based on vector
similarity
3. LLM Tool Selection: Used for situations that require calling external APIs. The LLM
determines, based on the user request and available API list, whether to use an external
API and which API to use.

scenarios, such as multi-path chain reasoning, dual-Agent review, tree-structured reasoning,
etc. The multi-path chain reasoning technique of this framework is derived from the paper Self-
Consistency Improves Chain Of Thought Reasoning In Language Models, which enhances the Agent’s
self-consistency and thereby improves performance by using multiple reasoning paths with the
same logic but different temperature coefficients. The dual-Agent review technique is based on
the paper Communicative Agents for Software Development, which sets up two Agents with different
behavioral logics to discuss the same task and takes the agreed-upon conclusion as the output,
reducing hallucinations and intellectual limitations of a single Agent. Tree-structured reasoning
originates from the paper Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with LLMs and is suitable
for tree-based reasoning scenarios, supporting inference methods such as breadth-first search.

existing Agent frameworks LangFlow and Flowise at the initial stage of framework design. It was
found that both frameworks are essentially graphical interfaces for LangChain, without additional
abstraction or encapsulation. For non-developers (industry experts), LangFlow and Flowise

results. For developers, the cost reduction brought by framework simplification is limited, while
the inflexibility of the frameworks adds extra workload. The core issue with these frameworks

costs while solving real-world problems, whereas non-developers hope to be able to build usable
applications independently without development skills.

Privileged identities are a critical component in modern security strategies, particularly for
organizations utilizing cloud and hybrid environments. These identities refer to accounts or
users that are granted elevated permissions, enabling them to perform sensitive operations,
such as managing user access, configuring systems, or administering critical resources.
Because these accounts hold the keys to an organization's most important assets, their
management must be robust, systematic, and auditable.
Effective management of privileged identities involves several best practices. Firstly, access
should be granted only when absolutely necessary, following the principle of least privilege.
This means limiting the scope and duration of elevated access, so that users only have the
necessary idx_216ef8f9 permissions for the task at hand and only for as long as needed. Microsoft Entra
Privileged Identity Management (PIM) facilitates this by providing just-in-time and time-
bound access, requiring approval workflows, and enforcing multi-factor authentication for role
activation. Additionally, regular access reviews and justification requests ensure that privileges
are not retained longer than required, reducing the risk of misuse or compromise.
By centralizing and automating the management of privileged identities, organizations can
significantly reduce their attack surface, maintain compliance with regulatory requirements,
and improve overall security posture.

Introduction to privileged identities
Privileged identities are specialized accounts or users within an organization that have been
granted elevated permissions, allowing them to perform critical and sensitive operations that
go beyond idx_1a49506e what standard users can do. These identities are central to the administration of IT
systems, cloud services, and data resources because they have the authority to manage user
access, configure infrastructure, oversee system security, and even alter or delete vital data. In a
modern business environment the concept of privileged identities has become a cornerstone in
the defense against cyber threats and the assurance of regulatory compliance.
Service accounts used by applications to access databases or perform automated tasks may
also be considered privileged if they are granted broad access rights. Because these identities
hold the "keys to the kingdom," they are highly attractive targets for cyber attackers. If
compromised, a privileged account can be used to escalate attacks, exfiltrate sensitive data, or
disrupt business operations on a large scale.

Data storage (raw)
Unlike operational databases such as Azure SQL or PostgreSQL—which are optimized for structured,
transactional workloads—raw storage solutions such as Azure Blob Storage, Azure Data Lake
Storage (ADLS), or Microsoft OneLake are designed to store large volumes of unstructured or
semi-structured data efficiently. These storage systems serve as cost-effective repositories for
data that may later be transformed, analyzed, or processed in downstream analytics pipelines.
Azure Files and Azure NetApp Files can be used as recipients of data transformations (for example,
reports) that can be shared across applications through mounted volumes. Azure NetApp Files
is particularly suited for very high-throughput and ultra-low latency workloads. Blob Storage is
widely used across data and non-data applications for storing raw binary objects. ADLS builds
on the same underlying service but introduces a true hierarchical namespace and is therefore
optimized for data operations.
Serving and data visualization
The data serving and visualization layers are distinct yet closely related components. The serving
layer exposes processed, analyzed, or transformed data to applications, services, and users. The
visualization layer builds on this by presenting the data through dashboards, reports, charts, and
other graphical formats. Power BI—now integrated into Microsoft Fabric—is the flagship service
for data visualization, designed to empower business users with self-service analytics. Power
BI enables the creation of reports and dashboards, which can also be easily added to external
applications using Power BI Embedded. Azure Data Explorer dashboards provide lightweight
visualization capabilities, particularly suited for real-time telemetry and log analytics scenarios.
While they are developer-friendly, they are primarily optimized for operational monitoring,
troubleshooting, and time-series exploration—not general-purpose BI.
Other data capabilities
Azure AI Search is a general-purpose search service increasingly used as a vector database and a hybrid
search engine, combining the strengths of both vector- and keyword-based search. While Cosmos DB
and Azure SQL also offer capabilities for full-text and vector search, Azure AI Search remains the most
versatile for search-centric scenarios due to its built-in support for semantic ranking, hybrid retrieval,
cognitive skills for content enrichment, and automatic indexing of data sources.
For time series data, Azure Data Explorer stands out as the most suitable service. It can ingest
billions of rows and respond to queries within milliseconds, making it ideal for high-throughput,
low-latency analytics.

Zooming in on HTAP
Traditionally, online transaction processing (OLTP) systems, such as relational databases, and
online analytical processing (OLAP) systems, such as data warehouses, are separated due to
their differing performance needs and data models. HTAP eliminates the need to separate these
workloads, enabling real-time analytics directly on live data. HTAP is transformative because it
eliminates the need to copy data, which is time-consuming to maintain, prone to staleness, and
can introduce inconsistencies.
Data Architecture 264
Additionally, in traditional architectures, application teams typically only consider their
operational system as the system of record, while data teams rely on the raw layer available in their
data lake. With HTAP, all teams can align on a single, shared data store as the authoritative source.
However, this advanced capability—long sought after by data architects—has yet to become
mainstream. As you can see in Figure 7.5, there are currently a handful of options.
Figure 7.5 – HTAP capabilities in Azure
Since true HTAP means that there should be no copy from the source system to an external analytical
one, the only fully compliant HTAP option (as of June 2025) in Azure is Synapse Link for Cosmos
DB, as Synapse directly interacts with the analytical store of Cosmos DB. The analytical store of
Cosmos DB must be enabled at the container level, and once done, Cosmos will automatically
sync the transactional store with its analytical store. Thanks to Synapse Link, we can query the
data using either Spark notebooks or SQL serverless endpoints. For best performance, you should
try to keep Synapse Link in the same region as your Cosmos DB.
